https://barragan.house.gov/2026/10/23/re: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 23, 2026 Contact: Jin.Choi@mail.house.gov WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, Rep. Nanette Barragán (CA-44) introduced the Coordinating Access, Research, and Education for Blood Cancer Act , or the CARE for Blood Cancer Act , bipartisan legislation to establish a National Blood Cancer Program within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The program would strengthen public awareness, improve health professional training, expand research on diagnostics and treatments, and support individuals and caregivers affected by blood cancer. Blood cancers account for approximately 10 percent of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States, and someone in the country dies from a blood cancer approximately every nine minutes. Despite their significant impact, blood cancer symptoms can be difficult to recognize, and there is no routine screening method that can universally detect all blood cancers. While advances in treatment have improved outcomes for many patients, barriers to accessing effective care remain. “Everyone living with blood cancer deserves the opportunity to live a longer, healthier life,” said Rep. Barragán. “My sister is a multiple myeloma thriver, so I have seen firsthand how too many patients and families face the challenges of a blood cancer diagnosis without the information, support, and access to care they need. The CARE for Blood Cancer Act is a bipartisan bill that would bring federal agencies together to increase education among both the public and providers, fund more innovative research, and help ensure patients can access the diagnostics and treatments that can make a difference in their lives.” The CARE for Blood Cancer Act would direct HHS to coordinate with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), and other federal agencies to establish a comprehensive national approach to blood cancer education, detection, and treatment. Specifically, the legislation would: Expand public awareness and provider education: Provide grants to state, local, territorial, and Tribal health agencies to increase awareness of blood cancers in the community and health care workforce. Improve access to diagnostics and treatments: Provide grants to institutions of higher education and academic medical centers to improve the availability of, and access to, blood cancer diagnostics and treatments. Strengthen health professional training: Develop educational materials and programming to help health professionals better detect and treat blood cancers. “Nearly 1.8 million people in the United States are living with a blood cancer diagnosis,” said Gwen Nichols, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Blood Cancer United. “Although we have seen tremendous advancements in treatments and survival rates over the last several decades, there is still so much more to be done to find cures and relieve patients and their families from the burden of blood cancer. Blood Cancer United is proud to support the CARE for Blood Cancer Act, which would put more resources towards educating the public and healthcare providers on how to spot blood cancer earlier and invest in research to improve diagnostics and treatments. We are grateful to Rep. Barragan for her leadership on this issue and dedication to helping blood cancer patients and their families.” “Far too many people living with multiple myeloma and other blood cancers face unnecessary delays in diagnosis and barriers to accessing the care they need,” said Heather Cooper Ortner, President and CEO of the International Myeloma Foundation. “These challenges are often compounded for individuals in medically underserved communities, where disparities in access to timely, high-quality care can have profound consequences. The CARE for Blood Cancer Act represents an important step toward closing these gaps by equipping healthcare providers with the knowledge to recognize blood cancers earlier, increasing awareness among those at greatest risk, and helping more patients access timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment. We are grateful to Congresswoman Barragán for her leadership and longstanding commitment to improving the lives of people affected by blood cancers. The International Myeloma Foundation is proud to support this important legislation.” Original cosponsors for the bill include: Reps. Jim Costa (CA-21), Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-01), John Garamendi (CA-08), Jonathan Jackson (IL-01), Hank Johnson (GA-04), Doris Matsui (CA-07), LaMonica McIver (NJ-10), Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC-At Large), Pete Sessions (TX-17), Lateefah Simon (CA-12), and Rashida Tlaib (MI-12). https://barragan.house.gov/2026/10/20/re: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 20, 2026 Contact: Jin.Choi@mail.house.gov WASHINGTON, D.C. — Last week, Congresswoman Nanette Barragán (CA-44) reintroduced the National Patient Safety Board Act , legislation to establish a National Patient Safety Board (NPSB) within the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to identify widespread causes of patient harm and develop solutions to prevent medical errors and improve patient safety. An estimated one in four patients in the United States experiences some form of harm or adverse event in a health care setting. Preventable medical errors are estimated to contribute to approximately 250,000 deaths annually. These figures underscore the urgent need for a coordinated, nationwide approach to identifying risks and preventing avoidable harm before it occurs. “Our health care system must do more to protect patients and prevent medical errors that can have devastating, lifelong consequences,” said Rep. Barragán. “The National Patient Safety Board Act would bring experts, health care providers, government agencies, and private partners together to identify risks, develop effective solutions, and build safer health care systems for patients across the country.” Modeled after the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and the Commercial Aviation Safety Team (CAST), the NPSB would take a nonpunitive, collaborative approach to patient safety. The National Patient Safety Board would: Identify and anticipate patient harm: Help health care organizations adopt data surveillance technologies, including automated systems and artificial intelligence, to detect warning signs and emerging risks while reducing the burden of manual data collection on frontline health care workers. Investigate widespread safety risks: Prioritize major sources of harm and conduct multidisciplinary studies to understand their underlying causes and identify opportunities for prevention. Recommend solutions that save lives: Develop evidence-based recommendations and advance the use of technologies and automated safeguards that can help prevent medical errors and keep patients safe. “We are very excited to see the National Patient Safety Board Act re-introduced in the 119th Congress, and we thank Representative Nanette Barragan for her continued leadership as the sponsor of this visionary legislation,” said Martin Hatlie, Director of Policy and Advocacy for Patients for Patient Safety US. “Establishment of this non-regulatory, investigation body will fill an important gap in our nation’s learning and improvement engine, by creating a place where errors or systemic risks are studied to proactively prevent future harm. https://barragan.house.gov/2026/10/19/re: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 19, 2026 Contact: Jin.Choi@mail.house.gov WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, Rep. Nanette Barragán (CA-44) called on the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to provide answers about its August 2026 settlement with Zillow and Redfin, raising concerns about whether the agreement will restore competition in the online rental advertising market and help lower costs for renters. In a letter to FTC Chairman Ferguson, Rep. Barragán requested information about the Commission’s oversight of the settlement, including how it will ensure Redfin reenters the Internet Listing Services (ILS) rental advertising market as a meaningful competitor and how it will measure whether the agreement benefits renters and property managers. The FTC’s settlement addresses a 2025 agreement under which Redfin shut down its ILS rental advertising business. The Commission alleged that the agreement eliminated an important competitor, potentially leading to higher prices and worse terms for property managers while reducing competition for renters. The stakes are high: Zillow, CoStar, and Redfin collectively account for more than 85 percent of revenue earned by national rental listing sites, while 88 percent of rental advertisers rely on these platforms. Meanwhile, a record 22.7 million renter households spend more than 30 percent of their income on housing. “Renters are already struggling with the high cost of housing, and we cannot afford to let anticompetitive corporate agreements make the problem worse,” said Rep. Barragán. “The FTC must ensure this settlement does more than put promises on paper. We need real accountability, meaningful competition, and clear evidence that property managers and renters are benefiting.” The settlement requires Redfin to restart its ILS rental advertising business within six months after the final order is entered, invest millions of dollars in the business, hire dedicated personnel, and operate the business for multiple years. It also imposes obligations on Zillow intended to facilitate Redfin’s return to the market and protect customers’ ability to contract with Redfin. However, Zillow has publicly stated that its syndication partnership with Redfin will continue unchanged, raising questions about how the FTC will ensure Redfin can operate as an independent competitor while maintaining that relationship. Rep. Barragán’s letter seeks answers on 11 areas of oversight, including: Settlement status and deadlines: Whether the court has entered the final order and when Redfin’s six-month relaunch deadline begins. Compliance and enforcement: What documentation the FTC requires, how it will monitor compliance, and what penalties or other remedies are available if the companies fail to meet their obligations. Meaningful competition: How the FTC will evaluate Redfin’s ability to attract customers, secure listings, compete for advertising contracts, rebuild its sales operations, and operate independently of Zillow. Consumer and market impacts: Whether the FTC will track advertising prices, fees paid by property managers, market share, and other indicators of whether competition is improving. Corporate accountability: How the Commission will enforce protections for customer contracts and employee recruitment and review future agreements that could restrict competition. The letter also requests copies of Redfin’s compliance reports and other information that can legally be shared with Congress. If those materials cannot be provided, Rep. Barragán requests a briefing on the FTC’s assessment of the companies’ compliance and its ongoing monitoring efforts. Rep. Barragán requested a response from the Commission by December 1, 2026. The following Members of Congress have signed onto the letter: Rep. Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), Rep. Kathy Castor (FL-14), Rep. Yvette Clarke (NY-9), Rep. Yassamin Ansari (AZ-3), Rep. Rosa DeLauro (CT-3), Rep. Adelita Grijalva (AZ-7), and Rep. Greg Stanton (AZ-4). The full text of the letter can be found HERE . ###

https://barragan.house.gov/2026/10/02/as: As new cuts kick in, 5 million have already lost SNAP after initial Trump cuts FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 2, 2026 Contact: Jin.Choi@mail.house.gov Washington, D.C. – Today, Congresswoman Barragán (CA-44) warned that another SNAP cut from H.R. 1, the Republican Reconciliation Law, has gone into effect. The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) is federally funded and administered by states. H.R. 1 cut the federal share of funding for SNAP administrative costs in half, meaning that states are now required to cover 75% of SNAP administrative costs. Those cuts became effective on October 1, 2026. Nationwide, this represents over $16 billion in reduced funding for SNAP. In California, this means the state will have to pay at least $670 million more to keep the program operating. For state-by-state estimates of SNAP funding cuts effective today, click here . The reduction of administrative funding leaves states with fewer resources to process applications, determine eligibility, and ensure families receive the benefits they are eligible for. This massive funding cut also jeopardizes other state and local services as states struggle to replace this lost funding. A similar cost shift, cutting federal payments to states for SNAP benefits, will go into effect October 1, 2027. “Donald Trump and Republicans chose to give tax breaks to billionaires while making it harder for working families to put food on the table,” said Congresswoman Barragán. “ Now, they are forcing states to pick up the tab for SNAP as they pile on new requirements and red tape onto a program that millions of Americans rely on to feed their families. That is the wrong choice, and families in California are paying the price. No parent should have to worry about whether they can afford their next meal because Republicans decided billionaires needed another tax break. I will continue fighting to reverse these cruel cuts, protect SNAP, and make sure families—not billionaires—are our priority.” “Trump and Republicans in Congress passed tax breaks for millionaires and billionaires on the backs of families who are already struggling to afford sky-high grocery costs. Over 5 million Americans have already lost SNAP food assistance because of Trump’s cuts, and today, another SNAP cut from the Big Ugly Law kicks in. Trump and Republicans have handed states huge SNAP funding cuts, with more cuts coming next year. Worse still, these administrative cuts are coming as Republicans have also made SNAP more difficult to access. They’ve created new paperwork and new requirements, then cut the funding used to enroll people. Congress must fix these cuts through the Farm Bill and protect families who rely on SNAP to keep food on the table,” said Congresswoman Shontel Brown , Vice Ranking Member on the House Agriculture Committee . According to USDA data, more than 5 million Americans , including about 2 million children, have already lost SNAP since H.R. 1 was enacted in July 2025. In California, over 330,000 have lost SNAP coverage in the last year. H.R.1’s SNAP cuts were enacted alongside cuts to Medicaid and other programs to pay for tax cuts that overwhelmingly benefited large corporations and the wealthiest Americans. The Republican Farm Bill which passed the House and is currently under consideration in the Senate, locks in $187 billion in SNAP cuts. Republicans rejected all Democratic attempts to roll back SNAP cuts in the House Farm Bill . ###
https://barragan.house.gov/2026/09/23/re: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE September 23, 2026 Contact: Jin.Choi@mail.house.gov WASHINGTON, D.C. — On Monday, Congresswoman Nanette Barragán (CA-44) welcomed the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s issuance of a direct final rule, which updates federal regulations to clarify scientifically appropriate non-animal methods can be used to evaluate the safety of drugs and biological products before they are tested in humans. The FDA’s action follows bipartisan congressional efforts led by Rep. Barragán and Rep. Buddy Carter (R-Ga.) to ensure the agency fully implements the authority Congress established through the FDA Modernization Act 2.0. In April 2025, Barragán and Carter introduced the FDA Modernization Act 3.0 , legislation requiring FDA to publish a final rule updating its regulations to reflect the availability of non-animal testing methods. The bill was cosponsored by Reps. Diana Harshbarger (R-Tenn.), Troy Carter (D-La.), Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), and Vern Buchanan (R-Fla.). “Modern science is giving us better tools to understand how medicines affect people, and our laws and regulations need to keep pace,” said Congresswoman Nanette Barragán . “I’m proud to have worked across the aisle to advance the FDA Modernization Act 3.0 and help ensure that FDA’s regulations reflect the scientific tools available today. This action is an important step toward giving researchers greater flexibility to use validated methods that can improve drug development while maintaining rigorous safety standards.” “This is a long-delayed but highly consequential move by FDA to bring drug-development regulations into the 21st century,” said Wayne Pacelle, president of the Center for a Humane Economy and Animal Wellness Action . “The agency knocking down outdated regulatory language propping up ineffective animal testing strategies put new methods rooted in human biology. Over time, we’ll see better, safer, less costly drugs that help people struggling with disease.” The FDA’s new rule updates terminology and removes language that could suggest animal testing is the only acceptable approach for generating safety information for human drugs and biological products. The agency said the rule recognizes a broader range of approaches, including methods involving human cells, organs-on-chips, computer models, and other New Approach Methodologies (NAMs). The rule does not prohibit animal studies or change existing evidentiary standards. FDA stated that non-animal methods may be used when they are adequately validated and appropriate for the product and regulatory question. The FDA’s action is being issued as a direct final rule and is subject to public comment. The full bill text can be found HERE . ###

https://barragan.house.gov/2026/09/17/re: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE September 17, 2026 Contact: Jin.Choi@mail.house.gov WASHINGTON, D.C. – Yesterday, Congresswoman Nanette Barragán (CA-44) introduced the Housing Tariff Exclusion Act , legislation to help lower the cost of building new homes, by creating a targeted process to exclude certain homebuilding materials from tariffs when domestic supply cannot meet demand. At a time when communities across the country are struggling with a shortage of housing, higher construction costs can make it even harder to build the homes families need. Estimates of the national housing shortage vary by methodology, with recent estimates ranging from roughly 3 million to 5 million homes. “Families are already facing the high cost of buying or renting a home. We should not make it more expensive to build the homes our communities need,” said Rep. Barragán . “Tariffs can raise construction costs, which in turn hurt the number of homes available for the Americans who need it most. The Housing Tariff Exclusion Act takes a targeted approach by giving the federal government a process to provide relief when domestic production simply cannot keep pace. We need to make it easier—not more expensive—to build housing in America.” “With the nation in the midst of a housing affordability crisis, the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) commends Rep. NanetteBarragán (D-Calif.) for introducing legislation to help lower housing costs,” said NAHB Chairman Bill Owens. “Tariffs on building materials are driving up construction costs and putting homeownership further out of reach for families. The Housing Tariff Exclusion Act would help relieve these cost pressures by creating a process to exempt key building materials from tariffs, giving businesses greater certainty and helping make housing more affordable.” “The National Lumber and Building Material Dealers Association (NLBMDA) is proud to support the Housing Tariff Exclusion Act and thanks Representative Barragán for her leadership on this issue. Recent trade actions have placed additional pressure on the cost and availability of essential building materials at a time when improving housing affordability is a national priority,” said Jonathan M. Paine, CAE, President & CEO of NLBMDA. “Congress recognized through its recent bipartisan housing legislation that expanding supply is central to improving affordability. The Housing Tariff Exclusion Act carries that work forward by addressing tariffs that increase the cost of essential building materials. By establishing an exclusion process for critical homebuilding materials, this legislation would provide greater certainty for dealers and builders, ease construction cost pressures and support the increased housing production needed to improve affordability nationwide.” A December 2025 analysis from the Center for American Progress estimated that tariffs on homebuilding materials could add approximately $17,500 to the cost of building a new home and contribute to roughly 450,000 fewer homes being built through 2030 . The legislation would: Require the Secretary of Commerce to establish a process for businesses to request exclusions for homebuilding materials, including expedited exclusions for critical homebuilding products; Require the Secretary to exclude tariffs on qualifying homebuilding products when domestic supply or production capacity cannot meet demand; Apply the process to qualifying tariffs implemented since January 19, 2025, while excluding antidumping, countervailing, and Section 201 safeguard duties; Allow qualifying imports to receive the lower tariff rate when an exclusion is granted; Sunset the Secretary’s exclusion authority on October 1, 2029, while allowing previously granted exclusions to remain in effect; and Exclude the 15 rare earth elements identified in the legislation from the process due to separate national security considerations. The Housing Tariff Exclusion Act would give builders and businesses greater certainty while maintaining a process focused on domestic supply, market demand, and the specific needs of the housing construction industry. Barragán and Joyce introduce Bipartisan Legislation to Improve Access to Innovative Treatments for Seniors and People with Disabilities WASHINGTON, D.C.– Yesterday, Representatives Nanette Barragán (D-CA) and John Joyce, M.D. (R-PA) reintroduced the bipartisan Access to Innovative Treatments Act (AITA) , a bill that would improve access to promising new treatments for seniors and people with disabilities enrolled in Medicare. The bill would require the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) to reconsider certain Medicare coverage decisions in a timely manner when new evidence of a drug’s effectiveness becomes available, and ensures that drugs are evaluated on an individual basis, rather than as part of a broad class. AITA does not require coverage or reimbursement of any specific drug. It instead ensures Medicare coverage decisions are based on the best available evidence and revisited as data evolves, giving patients a fairer opportunity to access innovative therapies when they need them most. This could lead to the lower out-of-pocket costs for new, expensive drugs that get covered under Medicare. The bill addresses concerns following CMS’ decision in 2022 to deny Medicare coverage of certain FDA-approved, Alzheimer’s treatments unless patients were enrolled in clinical trials, which caused confusion and restricted access— particularly for individuals in rural and underserved communities. “Patients should not be denied access to promising treatments simply because of outdated or overly broad coverage decisions. The Access to Innovative Treatments Act is necessary to ensure that Medicare keeps pace with the latest science— it creates accountability by establishing a timeline to review new evidence and giving every treatment a fair, individualized review. Thank you to Dr. Joyce for joining me to put patients first and make sure seniors and people with disabilities have a real opportunity to benefit from medical innovation, no matter where they live or what type of insurance they have,” said Congresswoman Nanette Barragán. “Approximately 282,000 Pennsylvanians are living with Alzheimer’s disease, and that number is expected to grow significantly in the years ahead. Unfortunately, access to treatments and care is not keeping pace. This legislation calls on CMS to provide coverage for emerging therapies that have demonstrated effectiveness, ensuring patients have access to options that can improve quality of life, help slow the progression of this devastating disease, and provide hope for patients and their families. I thank Congresswoman Barragán for her continued partnership in addressing this challenging reality faced by millions of Americans seeking solutions and support,” said Congressman John Joyce, M.D. “The Access to Innovative Treatments Act would ensure Medicare coverage decisions are made based on a treatment’s own clinical evidence — not broad, class-wide restrictions that create unnecessary barriers to FDA-approved therapies,’ said Rachel Conant, Alzheimer’s Association Senior Vice President of Public Policy and AIM executive director. ‘We are grateful to Reps. Barragán and Joyce for their longstanding commitment to the Alzheimer’s community and their bipartisan leadership on this issue. For people living with Alzheimer’s, the window to benefit from treatment is limited — delays in access have real consequences, and this legislation would help ensure patients can reach FDA-approved therapies when they matter most.” “In 2022, one in five adults aged 65 and older skipped, delayed, or rationed prescription treatments due to concerns about the out-of-pocket costs they would incur at the pharmacy counter,” said Scott Frey, Senior Vice President of Public Policy & Government Relations for the Alliance for Aging Research. “Those cost challenges have only been exacerbated in recent years as patients balance their healthcare needs against rising costs for other essential goods. The Alliance champions the Access to Innovative Treatments Act because we recognize the critical need to make healthcare more affordable and accessible for Americans, especially those who rely on prescription drugs to manage chronic and complex diseases.” “People living with Alzheimer’s cannot afford unnecessary delays in accessing FDA-approved treatments that may help slow the progression of this devastating disease,” said Catherine Patterson, Acting Chief Operating Officer, UsAgainstAlzheimer’s . ”We thank Representatives John Joyce and Nanette Barragán for their leadership on the Access to Innovative Treatments Act, which helps ensure Medicare coverage decisions keep pace with evolving clinical evidence. By creating a more transparent and accountable process for reconsidering coverage as new data emerge, and by evaluating therapies on an individual basis, this legislation puts patients and their families first. UsAgainstAlzheimer’s is proud to support this important effort to expand timely access to treatments.” The following organizations have endorsed the bill: Alzheimer’s Association, Alzheimer’s Impact Movement (AIM), Alliance for Aging Research, National Hispanic Council on Aging (NHCOA), UsAgainstAlzheimer’s. Barragán had shared her own mother’s experience navigating Medicare and Medicaid, through which access to the glucose monitoring technology was limited until her condition worsened. Currently, Medicare coverage of CGMs is limited to individuals with diabetes who use insulin or individuals who can document severe hypoglycemic events— criteria that exclude the majority of Medicare beneficiaries living with diabetes. “Our healthcare system is failing patients by waiting until it is too late to act,” said Congresswoman Barragán. “We should be investing in prevention, not just treatment. Continuous glucose monitors give patients the ability to manage their health in real time and avoid life-threatening complications. Expanding access to CGMs is a commonsense step that will save lives and reduce long-term health care costs. I thank Secretary Kennedy for his willingness to work with Congress and solve this problem. We have the tools and the evidence—now we need the policy to match.” Diabetes affects more than 38 million Americans, including approximately one in three Medicare beneficiaries, and costs the U.S. healthcare system over $400 billion annually. Individuals with diabetes face medical expenses more than twice as high as those without the condition, largely due to preventable complications. CGMs are a major advancement in diabetes care, which allow patients to track glucose in real time, reduce dangerous hypoglycemic events, and lowers hospitalizations and emergency room visits—key drivers of Medicare spending. In her letter, Rep. Barragán called on HHS and CMS to: Use its existing regulatory authority to expand Medicare coverage of CGMs to all beneficiaries with diabetes; and Provide a detailed update on steps being taken to improve access to glucose monitoring technologies for Medicare and Medicaid patients. https://barragan.house.gov/2026/04/30/re: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE April 30, 2026 Contact: Jin.Choi@mail.house.gov WASHINGTON, D.C.– Congresswoman Nanette Barragán (CA-44) and Congressman Neal Dunn (FL-02) introduced H.R. 8500, the Ensuring Timely Access to Coverage Decisions Act, bipartisan legislation aimed at improving Medicare patients’ access to timely and appropriate care. Currently, Medicare beneficiaries experience delays and unnecessary administrative hurdles in seeking coverage decisions through the local coverage determination process due to inconsistent standards and a lack of transparency. This legislation would increase stakeholder involvement, require timely completion of requests, and create a formal review process for reconsideration decisions. Congresswoman Barragán said, “Too often, seniors and people with disabilities face long delays or inconsistencies in Medicare covering innovative medical devices or treatments that could improve their quality of life. That is why I am co-leading the bipartisan Timely Access to Coverage Decisions Act with Congressman Dunn and Congresswoman Tenney, which would make the Medicare coverage decision process more timely, transparent, and better backed by clinical expertise. This bill is an important step to helping ensure Medicare enrollees can access the appropriate care they need, when they need it.” “Americans on Medicare too often face unnecessary delays and red tape in seeking coverage determinations for needed care. This bipartisan legislation will work to ensure patients receive timely coverage decisions and improve access to quality care,” said Congressman Dunn. “I thank Congresswoman Barragán for her work on this bipartisan legislation to bring fairness to Medicare coverage.” ###
